claim: The study involved 108 human embryos obtained from the Medical Research Council (MRC)/Wellcome Human Developmental Biology Resource, spanning Carnegie stages (CS) 10–18.
source: The study involved 108 human embryos (Table 1), obtained from the Medical Research Council (MRC)/Wellcome Human Developmental Biology Resource (https://www.hdbr.org/), with UK ethics committee approval.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of embryos and their source in the Results section.

claim: All embryos in the study were chromosomally and morphologically normal.
source: All embryos in the study were chromosomally and morphologically normal, and were assigned to CS, as described (O'Rahilly and Muller, 1987; Bullen and Wilson, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that all embryos were chromosomally and morphologically normal.

claim: Primary neurulation is completed at the posterior neuropore with neural plate bending that is similar, but not identical, to the mouse.
source: Primary neurulation is completed at the posterior neuropore with neural plate bending that is similar, but not identical, to the mouse.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Secondary neurulation proceeds from CS13 with formation of a single lumen as in mouse, not coalescence of multiple lumens as in chick.
source: Secondary neurulation proceeds from CS13 with formation of a single lumen as in mouse, not coalescence of multiple lumens as in chick.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: There is no evidence of a 'transition zone' from primary to secondary neurulation in human embryos.
source: There is no evidence of a 'transition zone' from primary to secondary neurulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Secondary neural tube 'splitting' occurs in 60% of proximal human tail regions.
source: Secondary neural tube 'splitting' occurs in 60% of proximal human tail regions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: A somite is formed every 7 hr in human embryos.
source: A somite is formed every 7 hr in human, compared with 2 hr in mice and a 5 hr 'segmentation clock' in human organoids.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: A somite is formed every 2 hr in mice.
source: A somite is formed every 7 hr in human, compared with 2 hr in mice and a 5 hr 'segmentation clock' in human organoids.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract, citing known data about mice.

claim: Human organoids have a 5 hr 'segmentation clock'.
source: A somite is formed every 7 hr in human, compared with 2 hr in mice and a 5 hr 'segmentation clock' in human organoids.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract, citing known data about human organoids.

claim: Termination of axial elongation occurs after down-regulation of WNT3A and FGF8 in the CS15 embryonic tailbud.
source: Termination of axial elongation occurs after down-regulation of WNT3A and FGF8 in the CS15 embryonic tailbud, with a 'burst' of apoptosis that may remove neuro-mesodermal progenitors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: A 'burst' of apoptosis may remove neuro-mesodermal progenitors at the time of termination of axial elongation.
source: Termination of axial elongation occurs after down-regulation of WNT3A and FGF8 in the CS15 embryonic tailbud, with a 'burst' of apoptosis that may remove neuro-mesodermal progenitors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Abstract as a main finding of the study, with speculative language ('may').

claim: Open spina bifida (myelomeningocele) results from defective closure of the primary neural tube, most often at lumbar and upper sacral levels.
source: Open spina bifida (also called myelomeningocele) results from defective closure of the primary neural tube, most often at lumbar and upper sacral levels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Neuroepithelial damage and loss in open spina bifida is due to prolonged exposure to amniotic fluid.
source: Subsequent neuroepithelial damage and loss due to prolonged exposure to amniotic fluid (Stiefel et al., 2007) leads to a defect that is disabling in most individuals (Copp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Closed 'dysraphic' conditions arise at lower sacral and coccygeal levels of the body axis and result from disturbance of secondary neurulation.
source: Closed 'dysraphic' conditions arise at lower sacral and coccygeal levels of the body axis and result from disturbance of secondary neurulation, in which the neural tube forms without formation of neural folds.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: In secondary neurulation, the neural tube forms without formation of neural folds.
source: Closed 'dysraphic' conditions arise at lower sacral and coccygeal levels of the body axis and result from disturbance of secondary neurulation, in which the neural tube forms without formation of neural folds.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: In normal primary and secondary neurulation, the neural tube forms by closure and canalisation respectively.
source: In normal primary and secondary neurulation, the neural tube forms by closure and canalisation respectively (summarised in Figure 1 of Nikolopoulou et al., 2017), with extensive studies of both processes in experimental animals, especially chick, mouse, and rat.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Neurulation-stage human embryos span 3–7 weeks post-conception.
source: Despite the relative inaccessibility of neurulation-stage human embryos (3–7 weeks post-conception), a number of studies have described the anatomical, histological, and ultrastructural features of secondary neurulation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction.

claim: A population of self-renewing stem cells, termed neuro-mesodermal progenitors (NMPs), resides in the caudal-most embryonic region (the tailbud).
source: A population of self-renewing stem cells, termed neuro-mesodermal progenitors (NMPs), resides in the caudal-most embryonic region (the tailbud), with NMPs giving rise to neural and mesodermal derivatives, including the secondary neural tube and somites (Henrique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: NMPs give rise to neural and mesodermal derivatives, including the secondary neural tube and somites.
source: A population of self-renewing stem cells, termed neuro-mesodermal progenitors (NMPs), resides in the caudal-most embryonic region (the tailbud), with NMPs giving rise to neural and mesodermal derivatives, including the secondary neural tube and somites (Henrique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: NMP maintenance is required for axial elongation, mediated via an interplay between WNT3A and FGF8 expression, which promotes NMP survival in the tailbud.
source: NMP maintenance is required for axial elongation, mediated via an interplay between WNT3A and FGF8 expression, which promotes NMP survival in the tailbud.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Endogenous retinoic acid promotes differentiation and regulates body length.
source: Conversely, endogenous retinoic acid promotes differentiation and regulates body length (Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Two CS12 human embryos with open posterior neuropores were identified by microscopic inspection at collection.
source: In two intact CS12 embryos (Figure 1A and B; crown-rump length: 3 mm; 22–23 somites), we identified an open PNP by microscopic inspection at collection (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The neural plate is relatively flat in the most caudally located sections of CS12 embryos with open PNP, although incipient dorsolateral hinge points (DLHPs) are visible.
source: The neural plate is relatively flat in the most caudally located sections, although incipient dorsolateral hinge points (DLHPs) are visible (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The notochord underlies the neural plate midline in CS12 embryos with open PNP.
source: The notochord underlies the neural plate midline, and the caudal end of the hindgut is visible beneath the notochord in one embryo (Figure 1E), but not the other (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: In more rostral sections of CS12 embryos with open PNP, close to the 'zippering' point of PNP closure, elevated neural folds flank a marked ventral midline bend in the neural plate, the median hinge point (MHP), which precisely overlies the notochord.
source: In more rostral sections, close to the 'zippering' point of PNP closure, elevated neural folds flank a marked ventral midline bend in the neural plate, the median hinge point (MHP), which precisely overlies the notochord (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: DLHPs are situated where the neural plate changes from basal contact with surface ectoderm to basal contact with paraxial mesoderm in human CS12 embryos.
source: As in the mouse (McShane et al., 2015), the DLHPs are situated where the neural plate changes from basal contact with surface ectoderm to basal contact with paraxial mesoderm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: MHP and DLHPs characterise PNP closure in human embryos at CS12, marking a direct equivalence to Mode 2 spinal neurulation in the mouse embryo.
source: We conclude that MHP and DLHPs characterise PNP closure in human embryos at CS12, marking a direct equivalence to Mode 2 spinal neurulation in the mouse embryo (Shum and Copp, 1996).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion with citation support.

claim: Closure of the PNP is completed in human embryos around the 30-somite stage.
source: Hence, closure of the PNP is completed in human embryos around the 30-somite stage, as also reported for outbred mouse strains (Copp et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: There were no obvious differences in PNP closure rate or timing between female (n=24) and male (n=16) embryos.
source: There were no obvious differences in closure rate or timing between female (n=24) and male (n=16) embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: Crown-rump length increased 2.5-fold during CS13-18, from a mean value of 6.4 mm at CS13 to 15.4 mm at CS18.
source: Crown-rump length increased 2.5-fold during this period, from a mean value of 6.4 mm at CS13 to 15.4 mm at CS18 (Table 2; Figure 2J).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 2J.

claim: The PNP is closed in most embryos by CS13.
source: Observations on the intact embryos showed that the PNP is closed in most embryos by CS13, and a developing tailbud is present which exhibits mild ventral curvature and a thick rounded tip (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At CS13, somites are visible proximal to the tailbud, with an intervening region of presomitic mesoderm.
source: Somites are visible proximal to the tailbud (arrowheads in Figure 2C), with an intervening region of presomitic mesoderm at CS13 (yellow bracket in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By CS16, the somites extend almost to the tail tip.
source: By CS16, however, the somites extend almost to the tail tip (yellow arrow in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: As development progresses, the tail continues to lengthen but simultaneously narrows, particularly at the tip, to yield a sharply pointed structure by CS16.
source: As development progresses, striking changes occur in the tail which continues to lengthen (Table 2) but simultaneously narrows, particularly at the tip, to yield a sharply pointed structure by CS16 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D-F and Table 2.

claim: Subsequent to CS16, the tail shortens.
source: Subsequent to CS16, the tail shortens (Figure 2G; Table 2), and its distal portion becomes increasingly translucent in appearance.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2G and Table 2.

claim: By CS18, only a short, curved stump remains of the tail, and the tail is lost completely thereafter.
source: By CS18, only a short, curved stump remains (Figure 2H), and the tail is lost completely thereafter.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Between CS10 and CS13, during PNP closure, somite number increases approximately linearly with days of gestation.
source: Between CS10 and CS13, during PNP closure, somite number increases approximately linearly with days of gestation (Figure 1K): mean (± SD) somite numbers were: 8.0±1.4 at CS10, 18.4±2.6 at CS11, 23.5±3.4 at CS12, and 30.0±2.8 at CS13.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The linear regression equation of somite number versus days of gestation gives an increase of 20.3 somites over a 6-day period, equating to the formation of 3.4 somites per gestational day, or a new somite every 7.1 hr (95% confidence intervals: 4.8, 10.4).
source: The linear regression equation of this relationship (Figure 1K) gives an increase of 20.3 somites over a 6-day period, equating to the formation of 3.4 somites per gestational day, or a new somite every 7.1 hr (95% confidence intervals: 4.8, 10.4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: A new somite forms every 2 hr in rat and mouse embryos.
source: This compares with formation of a new somite every 2 hr in rat and mouse embryos (Brown and Fabro, 1981; Tam, 1981), and a 5 hr periodicity observed for the human 'in vitro segmentation clock' in stem cell-derived presomitic mesoderm-like cells (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Matsuda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: A 5 hr periodicity is observed for the human 'in vitro segmentation clock' in stem cell-derived presomitic mesoderm-like cells.
source: This compares with formation of a new somite every 2 hr in rat and mouse embryos (Brown and Fabro, 1981; Tam, 1981), and a 5 hr periodicity observed for the human 'in vitro segmentation clock' in stem cell-derived presomitic mesoderm-like cells (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Matsuda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Following PNP closure at CS13, the largest somite number was at CS16 (36.6±1.2).
source: Following PNP closure at CS13, the largest somite number was at CS16 (36.6±1.2; Table 2), although there was no statistically significant increase between CS13 and CS16 (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 2K.

claim: By CS17 and 18, only 31–34 somites could be identified, a significant reduction in number.
source: By CS17 and 18, we could identify only 31–34 somites, a significant reduction in number (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Somite formation in humans occurs at a rate that is 3.5 times slower than in rodent embryos.
source: Hence, somite formation in humans occurs at a rate that is 3.5 times slower than in rodent embryos, and ceases after CS16.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: Somite formation ceases after CS16 in human embryos.
source: Hence, somite formation in humans occurs at a rate that is 3.5 times slower than in rodent embryos, and ceases after CS16.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: Subsequent somite number reduction suggests that shortening of the tail during regression involves loss of somites.
source: Subsequent somite number reduction suggests that shortening of the tail during regression involves loss of somites (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from the data in Table 2.

claim: Caspase-dependent apoptosis occurs during tail regression in human and mouse embryos.
source: Positive cells were readily identified in the tails of both species (Figure 3A–N), arguing for a role of caspase-dependent apoptosis during tail regression in human and mouse.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Principal sites of apoptotic cell death include the regressing tailgut and, most abundantly, the ventral mesoderm overlying the epithelial ventral ectodermal ridge.
source: Principal sites of apoptotic cell death include the regressing tailgut (Figure 3D and F) and, most abundantly, the ventral mesoderm overlying the epithelial ventral ectodermal ridge (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: TUNEL-positive cells were detected in both mouse and human tail sections.
source: We also detected terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labelling (TUNEL)-positive cells in both mouse and human tail sections (data not shown), further confirming the presence of apoptotic cells during tail development/regression.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: In mouse, the tailbud displays a stage-dependent burst of apoptotic cell death at E13.5, with absence of caspase 3-positive cells 12 hr earlier, at E13.0, and only occasional dying cells 12 hr later, at E14.0.
source: In mouse, the tailbud displays a stage-dependent burst of apoptotic cell death at E13.5 (arrows in J), with absence of caspase 3-positive cells 12 hr earlier, at E13.0 (I), and only occasional dying cells 12 hr later, at E14.0 (arrow in K).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Human embryonic tailbuds show a similar developmental sequence to the mouse, with absence of cell death at CS13, abundant dying cells at CS15 and cessation of cell death by CS18.
source: Human embryonic tailbuds show a similar developmental sequence to the mouse, with absence of cell death at CS13 (L), abundant dying cells at CS15 (arrows in M) and cessation of cell death by CS18 (N).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: In both mouse and human tails, there appears to be a 'burst' of apoptosis at the stage when tail growth ceases, and just before regression of internal structures gets underway.
source: Hence, in both mouse and human tails, there appears to be a 'burst' of apoptosis at the stage when tail growth ceases, and just before regression of internal structures gets underway.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: The proximal (rostral) part of the tailgut is reported to degenerate before the more distal (caudal) part in both rat and mouse.
source: While the human embryonic tail appears to regress from caudal to rostral (Figure 2), the proximal (rostral) part of the tailgut is reported to degenerate before the more distal (caudal) part in both rat (Butcher, 1929; Qi et al., 2000) and mouse (Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: The tailgut showed a marked caudal-to-rostral reduction in cross-sectional area in human embryos at CS14-15.
source: Strikingly, the tailgut showed the reverse trend, with a marked caudal-to-rostral reduction in cross-sectional area (Figure 4A, B, and D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tailgut nuclear number diminished from caudal to rostral in human embryos at CS14-15.
source: Tailgut nuclear number also diminished from caudal to rostral (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rostral-to-caudal loss of the tailgut may be a general phenomenon among mammalian embryos.
source: We conclude that rostral-to-caudal loss of the tailgut may be a general phenomenon among mammalian embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion with speculative language ('may be').

claim: FGF8 and WNT3A are developmentally regulated during axial elongation in chick and mouse embryos, with strong expression in the tailbud during elongation, and down-regulation before axial growth ceases.
source: These genes are developmentally regulated during axial elongation in chick and mouse embryos, with strong expression in the tailbud during elongation, and down-regulation before axial growth ceases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: Direct inactivation or indirect down-regulation of FGF8 and WNT3A leads to premature axial truncation.
source: Direct inactivation or indirect down-regulation of the genes leads to premature axial truncation (Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Strong expression of FGF8 was observed in the tailbud at CS12 and CS13 in human embryos.
source: In accordance with these findings, we observed strong expression of FGF8 in the tailbud at CS12 and CS13, as revealed in whole embryos (Figure 5A and B) and longitudinal sections through hybridised caudal regions (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: At CS14, FGF8 expression reduced dramatically so that only a small 'dot' of expression was detected in the tailbud.
source: At CS14, FGF8 expression reduced dramatically so that only a small 'dot' of expression was detected in the tailbud (Figure 5C and G), and by CS15 expression of FGF8 was no longer detectable in the tail (Figure 5D and H).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: By CS15, expression of FGF8 was no longer detectable in the tail.
source: At CS14, FGF8 expression reduced dramatically so that only a small 'dot' of expression was detected in the tailbud (Figure 5C and G), and by CS15 expression of FGF8 was no longer detectable in the tail (Figure 5D and H).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of WNT3A followed a similar pattern to FGF8 with strong expression in the tailbud at CS12, reduced expression intensity at CS13, a remaining 'dot' of tailbud expression at CS14, and no detectable WNT3A expression in the tail at CS15.
source: Expression of WNT3A followed a similar pattern with strong expression in the tailbud at CS12 (Figure 5I and M), reduced expression intensity at CS13 (Figure 5J and N), a remaining 'dot' of tailbud expression at CS14 (Figure 5K and O), and no detectable WNT3A expression in the tail at CS15 (Figure 5L and P).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of FGF8 and WNT3A mirrors the relationship seen in mouse and chick, with strong tailbud expression during active axial extension, and dramatic down-regulation of both genes before the onset of axial growth cessation.
source: We conclude that expression of FGF8 and WNT3A mirrors the relationship seen in mouse and chick, with strong tailbud expression during active axial extension, and dramatic down-regulation of both genes before the onset of axial growth cessation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: Down-regulation of FGF8 and WNT3A appears complete by CS15, even though the embryonic tail does not reach its maximum length until some days later, at CS16.
source: It is striking that down-regulation appears complete by CS15, even though the embryonic tail does not reach its maximum length until some days later, at CS16 (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: Down-regulation of Fgf8 and Wnt3a, well in advance of cessation of axial elongation, has also been observed in mouse embryos.
source: Down-regulation of Fgf8 and Wnt3a, well in advance of cessation of axial elongation, has also been observed in mouse embryos (Cambray and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: 9 out of 15 human embryonic tails showed multiple lumens in some transverse sections in the initial study of tail morphology.
source: In our initial study of tail morphology, 9 out of 15 human embryonic tails showed multiple lumens in some transverse sections (Figure 3G and H), whereas the other 6 exhibited only a single neural tube lumen.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: In a second group of serially sectioned tails, 6 out of 10 tails had regions of duplicated neural tube.
source: In a second group of serially sectioned tails (Figures 4 and 6), 6 out of 10 tails had regions of duplicated neural tube.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: A 60% (15/25) frequency of neural tube duplication was found in human embryonic tails.
source: Hence, we find a 60% (15/25) frequency of neural tube duplication, confirming previous findings of multiple neural tube lumens in many human embryonic tails (Bolli, 1966; Lemire, 1969; Saitsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with citation support.

claim: A single lumen was invariably noted in the distal-most portion of the neural tube, just rostral to the tailbud tip in human embryos at CS13–18.
source: In our initial series of human tails, a single lumen was invariably noted in the distal-most portion of the neural tube, just rostral to the tailbud tip (CS13–18; Figure 3L–N).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: Secondary neurulation in human produces a neural tube with a single lumen.
source: This was confirmed in the second series of 10 serially sectioned tails (CS14–15; Figure 6B, C, and D), thus demonstrating that secondary neurulation in human produces a neural tube with a single lumen.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: When multiple secondary neural tube lumens were visible in the embryonic tail, this was invariably located at more rostral levels of the tail.
source: When multiple secondary neural tube lumens were visible in the embryonic tail, this was invariably located at more rostral levels of the tail (Figure 3G and H; Figure 4C; Figure 6B', C'', and D''), with variation in location between embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Multiple secondary neural tube lumens in human embryonic tails likely represent splitting, which tends to occur rostrally and does not represent a secondary neurulation mechanism involving coalescence of multiple lumens, as in chick.
source: We conclude that multiple secondary neural tube lumens in human embryonic tails likely represent splitting, which tends to occur rostrally and does not represent a secondary neurulation mechanism involving coalescence of multiple lumens, as in chick.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: Humans resemble other mammals, including rat and mouse, in initially forming a single secondary neural tube lumen in the tailbud.
source: Humans therefore resemble other mammals, including rat and mouse, in initially forming a single secondary neural tube lumen in the tailbud.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: A systematic literature review generated a final list of 28 papers with primary data relating to caudal development in human embryos, spanning over 100 years of research.
source: This generated a long list of publications that was filtered to include only those with primary data relating to caudal development in human embryos. The final list comprises 28 papers (Supplementary file 1) that span over 100 years of research, from the early 1900s (Kunitomo, 1918; Streeter, 1919) to recent times (Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: The literature review work was based on at least 925 human embryos obtained from varying sources.
source: This work was based on at least 925 human embryos obtained from varying sources (Supplementary file 1) including induced termination of pregnancy for 'social' reasons (where most embryos are expected to be normal), as well as spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) and ectopic pregnancy, where embryonic abnormalities are likely to be frequent.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: In mouse embryos, three sequential 'modes' of spinal neurulation occur: in Mode 1, the upper spinal neural plate bends only at the midline (the MHP); in Mode 2, at intermediate spinal levels, bending is at both MHP and paired DLHPs; in Mode 3, immediately before final PNP closure, the MHP is lost and bending occurs only at DLHPs.
source: In mouse embryos, three sequential 'modes' of spinal neurulation occur (Shum and Copp, 1996): in Mode 1, the upper spinal neural plate bends only at the midline (the MHP); in Mode 2, at intermediate spinal levels, bending is at both MHP and paired DLHPs; in Mode 3, immediately before final PNP closure, the MHP is lost and bending occurs only at DLHPs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: 'Mode 2' neural plate bending may be typical of the late stages of human spinal neurulation.
source: This raises the possibility that 'Mode 2' neural plate bending is typical of the late stages of human spinal neurulation, and that 'Mode 3' is mouse-specific and not seen in humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a possibility.

claim: 'Mode 3' may be mouse-specific and not seen in humans.
source: This raises the possibility that 'Mode 2' neural plate bending is typical of the late stages of human spinal neurulation, and that 'Mode 3' is mouse-specific and not seen in humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a possibility.

claim: Sectioning analysis along the body axis of CS14–15 human embryos revealed continuity of the neural tube from proximal (primary neurulation) to distal (secondary neurulation) levels.
source: Our sectioning analysis along the body axis of CS14–15 human embryos revealed continuity of the neural tube from proximal (primary neurulation) to distal (secondary neurulation) levels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: It was not possible to locate with any certainty where the transition from primary to secondary neural tube had occurred in human embryos.
source: Indeed, it was not possible to locate with any certainty where the transition from primary to secondary neural tube had occurred.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: The lack of a transition zone in human embryos closely resembles the mouse.
source: This closely resembles the mouse (Shum and Copp, 1996), but contrasts with the chick where a 'transition zone' occurs between primary and secondary neurulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: In chick, a 'transition zone' occurs between primary and secondary neurulation where the primary (dorsal) and secondary (ventral) neural tubes overlap for a short length of the spinal axis.
source: This closely resembles the mouse (Shum and Copp, 1996), but contrasts with the chick where a 'transition zone' occurs between primary and secondary neurulation. The chick primary (dorsal) and secondary (ventral) neural tubes overlap for a short length of the spinal axis (Dryden, 1980) and cells ingressing at the node-streak border participate in a distinct 'junctional neurulation' process with essential function of the Prickle-1 gene (Dady et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The lack of any evidence for 'junctional neurulation' in the present study of human embryos casts doubt on the proposed developmental origin of a rare dysraphic defect where primary and secondary neural tubes are physically and functionally separated.
source: However, the lack of any evidence for 'junctional neurulation' in the present study of human embryos casts doubt on the proposed developmental origin of this rare dysraphic defect.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as an inference.

claim: Secondary neurulation in mouse and rat involves formation of a single 'rosette' structure caudally, in which cells aggregate ('condense') from the dorsal tailbud mesenchyme, with subsequent (more rostral) organisation of the cells around a single lumen.
source: Secondary neurulation in mouse and rat involves formation of a single 'rosette' structure caudally, in which cells aggregate ('condense') from the dorsal tailbud mesenchyme, with subsequent (more rostral) organisation of the cells around a single lumen.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Secondary neurulation in mouse and rat is driven by apical junction formation, not by cell death.
source: This process is driven by apical junction formation, not by cell death (Butcher, 1929; Schoenwolf, 1984; Kostović-Knezević et al., 1991; Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: In chick, a caudal-to-rostral sequence of events occurs in which several independent lumens arise in the dorsal tailbud mesenchyme and, at more rostral levels, these coalesce to form the single lumen of the secondary neural tube.
source: In chick, by contrast, a caudal-to-rostral sequence of events occurs in which several independent lumens arise in the dorsal tailbud mesenchyme and, at more rostral levels, these coalesce to form the single lumen of the secondary neural tube (Criley, 1969; Schoenwolf and Delongo, 1980; Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Coalescence of multiple lumens in chick is a cell intercalation process driven by TGFβ/SMAD3 signalling.
source: Coalescence is a cell intercalation process driven by TGFβ/SMAD3 signalling (Gonzalez-Gobartt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Multiple neural tube lumens have often been observed in the developing or regressing human tail.
source: Multiple neural tube lumens have often been observed in the developing or regressing tail (Bolli, 1966; Lemire, 1969; Hughes and Freeman, 1974; Fallon and Simandl, 1978; Saitsu et al., 2004; Pytel et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2014), whereas other studies identify only a single lumen (Müller and O'Rahilly, 1987; Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: In mice, neural tube duplication is part of several mutant phenotypes and, when present, is a sign of pathology.
source: In mice, neural tube duplication is part of several mutant phenotypes and, when present, is a sign of pathology (Cogliatti, 1986).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: 'Splitting' of the human secondary neural tube appears a common but not obligatory phenomenon, perhaps reflecting changes related to tail regression.
source: An intriguing observation is the presence of secondary neural tube splitting in apparently normal human embryos, whereas this is seen only under pathological conditions in rodents.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The tailgut is an extension of the hindgut, beginning caudal to the level of the cloacal plate (future anus), which is located ventral to somite 29 in the mouse.
source: The tailgut is an extension of the hindgut, beginning caudal to the level of the cloacal plate (future anus), which is located ventral to somite 29 in the mouse (Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The tailgut forms and then regresses in both tailed (mouse, rat) and non-tailed (chick, human) animals.
source: The tailgut forms and then regresses in both tailed (mouse, rat) and non-tailed (chick, human) animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Human tailgut loss has been described as involving rostral-to-caudal degeneration.
source: Interestingly, human tailgut loss has been described as involving rostral-to-caudal degeneration rather than a more intuitive caudal-to-rostral loss (Kunitomo, 1918; Fallon and Simandl, 1978).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The tailgut lumen persists longest at the tail tip in rat and mouse.
source: Consistent with this, the tailgut lumen persists longest at the tail tip in rat (Butcher, 1929; Qi et al., 2000) and mouse (Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Anatomical and histological studies in rat, mouse, and human often conclude that the tailgut originates by mesenchyme-to-epithelium transition of tailbud cells, in a manner similar to the origin of the secondary neural tube.
source: Anatomical and histological studies in rat, mouse, and human often conclude that the tailgut originates by mesenchyme-to-epithelium transition of tailbud cells, in a manner similar to the origin of the secondary neural tube (Švajger et al., 1985; Gajović et al., 1989; Gajović et al., 1993; Nievelstein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Some authors consider the tailgut to arise by caudally directed extension of the hindgut.
source: However, others consider the tailgut to arise by caudally directed extension of the hindgut (Jolly and Ferester-Tadie, 1936).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Grafting of the E10.5 mouse tailbud beneath the kidney capsule produced no evidence of gut epithelial differentiation, in contrast to primitive streak/tailbud fragments at E8.5 and E9.5 which regularly produced this derivative.
source: Grafting of the E10.5 mouse tailbud beneath the kidney capsule produced no evidence of gut epithelial differentiation, in contrast to primitive streak/tailbud fragments at E8.5 and E9.5 which regularly produced this derivative.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: The finding that E10.5 mouse tailbud grafts produce no gut epithelial differentiation is consistent with loss of gut-forming potential in the later stage tailbud.
source: This finding is consistent with loss of gut-forming potential in the later stage tailbud (Tam, 1984).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: A retrospective clonal analysis found gut endoderm only as part of rostrally derived clones, unlike neural tube and paraxial mesoderm that were represented in clones extending into the tailbud at E10.5.
source: A retrospective clonal analysis found gut endoderm only as part of rostrally derived clones, unlike neural tube and paraxial mesoderm that were represented in clones extending into the tailbud at E10.5 (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: NMPs are bipotential, forming neural and paraxial mesodermal derivatives, whereas the endodermal lineage is set aside separately, early in gastrulation.
source: This led to the idea that NMPs are bipotential, forming neural and paraxial mesodermal derivatives, whereas the endodermal lineage is set aside separately, early in gastrulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as an inference from cited work.

claim: The NMP population at the chordoneural hinge region of the tailbud is fated to form neural and mesodermal derivatives, but not tailgut.
source: These findings are consistent with results of DiI-based lineage tracing and tissue grafting experiments (Cambray and Wilson, 2002; Cambray and Wilson, 2007) which show that the NMP population at the chordoneural hinge region of the tailbud is fated to form neural and mesodermal derivatives, but not tailgut.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: There is a proliferative zone at the hindgut tip, which is required to generate the colon by caudally directed gut extension.
source: Further support for this concept comes from the finding of a proliferative zone at the hindgut tip, which is required to generate the colon by caudally directed gut extension (Garriock et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Termination of axial elongation occurs in embryos with fewer than 40 somites in human.
source: Termination of axial elongation is highly species-specific, occurring in embryos with fewer than 40 somites in human (Table 2), at ~52-somite stage in chick, and in embryos with 65 somites in rat and mouse (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with reference to Table 2.

claim: Termination of axial elongation occurs at ~52-somite stage in chick.
source: Termination of axial elongation is highly species-specific, occurring in embryos with fewer than 40 somites in human (Table 2), at ~52-somite stage in chick, and in embryos with 65 somites in rat and mouse (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Termination of axial elongation occurs in embryos with 65 somites in rat and mouse.
source: Termination of axial elongation is highly species-specific, occurring in embryos with fewer than 40 somites in human (Table 2), at ~52-somite stage in chick, and in embryos with 65 somites in rat and mouse (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The findings with human embryos support a shared mechanism of axial elongation termination across species, as expression of FGF8 and WNT3A are developmentally regulated in close relationship to the time-course of axial elongation, similar to that in rodent embryos.
source: Our findings with human embryos support a shared mechanism, as we find that expression of FGF8 and WNT3A are developmentally regulated in close relationship to the time-course of axial elongation, similar to that in rodent embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: Cessation of tail growth in the mouse has been linked to a burst of apoptosis in the tailbud around E13.5.
source: Moreover, cessation of tail growth in the mouse has been linked to a burst of apoptosis in the tailbud around E13.5 (Wilson et al., 2009), and we detected an analogous burst of apoptosis in the CS15 human tailbud.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: A similar mechanism may underlie growth termination of the much shorter human embryonic tail.
source: Hence, a similar mechanism may underlie growth termination of the much shorter human embryonic tail.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion with speculative language ('may').

claim: In previous studies, it was concluded that apoptosis occurs only in the human cranial embryonic region, and non-apoptotic ('necrotic-like') death of tail structures was identified in the regressing human tail.
source: In immunohistochemistry studies, it was concluded that apoptosis occurs only in the human cranial embryonic region, and non-apoptotic ('necrotic-like') death of tail structures was identified in the regressing human tail (Sapunar et al., 2001; Vilović et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Cell death during chick tail regression was shown to involve caspase-dependent apoptosis.
source: In contrast, cell death during chick tail regression was shown to involve caspase-dependent apoptosis (Miller and Briglin, 1996).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Caspase-dependent apoptosis is the predominant mode of cell loss during tissue regression in the tails of both mouse and human.
source: We conclude that caspase-dependent apoptosis is the predominant mode of cell loss during tissue regression in the tails of both mouse and human.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The findings of this study show a close parallel between human and rodent embryos in several features of low spinal development: completion of primary neurulation, transition to secondary neurulation, cellular mechanism of secondary neural tube formation, and molecular basis of cessation of tail elongation.
source: The findings of this study show a close parallel between human and rodent embryos in several features of low spinal development: completion of primary neurulation, transition to secondary neurulation, cellular mechanism of secondary neural tube formation, and molecular basis of cessation of tail elongation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Conclusions section.

claim: Some aspects of chick low spinal development are not represented in the human embryos, indicating the need for caution in extrapolating findings from birds and lower vertebrates to humans.
source: In contrast, some aspects of chick low spinal development – often cited as an accurate model for human – are not represented in the human embryos, indicating the need for caution in extrapolating findings from birds and lower vertebrates to humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Conclusions section.

claim: The main differences between human and mouse/rat tail development relate to timing.
source: The main differences between human and mouse/rat tail development relate to timing with, for example, formation of a new somite every 7 hr in humans, compared with 2 hr in mouse/rat, and termination of tail elongation at the 36- to 37-somite stage in human, compared with the 65-somite stage in tailed rodents.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Conclusions section.

claim: While tail regression occurs completely in human embryos, the tail of mouse/rat embryos also regresses partially, with loss of secondary neural tube and tailgut, despite maintenance of an overall tail structure.
source: While tail regression occurs completely in human embryos, it is noteworthy that the tail of mouse/rat embryos also regresses partially, with loss of secondary neural tube and tailgut, despite maintenance of an overall tail structure.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Conclusions section.

claim: Embryos were donated by women undergoing termination of pregnancy for 'social' reasons, in most cases by mifepristone/misoprostol-induced (medical) delivery, with a few intact embryos obtained by ultrasound-guided vacuum aspiration (surgical).
source: Embryos were donated by women undergoing termination of pregnancy for 'social' reasons, in most cases by mifepristone/misoprostol-induced (medical) delivery, with a few intact embryos obtained by ultrasound-guided vacuum aspiration (surgical).

source: Comparisons to mouse were with random-bred CD1 embryos, staged by embryonic (E) day, where E0.5 is the day following overnight mating.

claim: The recent claim of 'tail-loss' during human evolution, due to a genetic change in the TBXT gene, ignores the fact that tail development persists in humans, albeit during a specific stage of embryonic development.
source: Moreover, we note that the recent claim of 'tail-loss' during human evolution, due to a genetic change in the TBXT gene (Xia et al., 2024), ignores the fact that tail development persists in humans, albeit during a specific stage of embryonic development.
